title: Where in the Waters?
section: What is the Future of Food Security?
text:
What is the Future of Food Security?
Marine aquaculture has the potential to be a more sustainable option to create future food security than the alternative land-based approach as the rising human population is estimated to reach 10 billion by 2050 (Gentry et al, 2017). Traditional farming is highly resource intensive. Beef production uses 61.1kg of grain and 28 kg for pork production, while 1 kg of finfish would use less than 13.5 kg of grain (Hall et al. 2011). Despite the promising solution, there is very little known about the areas on where species can thrive and aquacultures can succeed. Gentry et al. calculated the growth performance index and spatially assessed the location for general growing potential for suitable fish and bivalves (2017).

title: Where in the Waters?
text:
Why the Ocean?
The Earth’s living space is represented by 99% of water by volume and the ocean contains 97%. For this reason, the United Nations has implemented a Sustainable Development Goal 14 (Life Below Water) to include ocean conservation and encourage marine resources to be utilized efficiently (2022). This also ties into other United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals 1 (No poverty) and 2 (Zero hunger). Marine aquaculture seeks to meet the protein demands with the ocean representing an opportunity for food production with its potential being regarded as mostly untapped in terms of a farming source(Gentry et al. 2017).

title: Where in the Waters?
text:
Set-up
The geospatial analysis ues a few packages to create a function for mapping out the suitable locations throughout the West Coast region, which uses the following:

tidyverse: R package for syntax and data structures
sf: Simple features represents all types of common vector geometry
tmap: Thematic maps handles vector and raster objects with ggplot grammar
terra: For spatial data analysis
kableExtra: to make nice HTML tables



Show code
library(tidyverse)
library(sf) # vector data
library(here)
library(tmap) # static or interactive maps
library(janitor) 
library(terra) # spatial data
library(kableExtra) # tables

title: Where in the Waters?
text:
Data
The table represents the datasets that are used throughout this analysis in order to discover the locations for potential aquaculture in the West Coast region.



Dataset
Description
Source




Bathymetry (depth)
Charecterize the depth of the ocean
General Bathymetric Chart of the ceans


Exclusive Exonomic Zones (West Coast Region)
Martitime boundaries use for the creation of species distribtion lists per country
Marine Regions


Average Annual Sea Surface Temperature
from the years 2008 to 2012 within the region
NOAA




Load and inspect data
The sea surface temperature (SST) came from NOAA in multiple data files from 2008 to 2012. The data files were individually loaded then stacked to create a single raster file. The other two files were simply read accourdingly.


Show code
# Read in data for the average SST
set_file <- c(
    here("posts", "2026-11-26-aquaculture", "data", "average_annual_sst_2008.tif"),
    here("posts", "2026-11-26-aquaculture", "data", "average_annual_sst_2009.tif"),
    here("posts", "2026-11-26-aquaculture", "data", "average_annual_sst_2010.tif"),
    here("posts", "2026-11-26-aquaculture", "data", "average_annual_sst_2011.tif"),
    here("posts", "2026-11-26-aquaculture", "data", "average_annual_sst_2012.tif")
)

# File path for SST data stack
sst <- rast(set_file)

# Load bathymetry data
depth <- rast(here("posts", "2026-11-26-aquaculture", "data", "depth.tif"))

# Load West Coast EEZ 
eez_data <- sf::st_read(here("posts", "2026-11-26-aquaculture", "data", "wc_regions_clean.shp"))


The average sea surface temperature over the 5 year period was calculated and converted from Kelvin to Celsius.


Show code
# single raster of average SST
sst_mean_c <- mean(sst, na.rm = TRUE) - 273.15


Depth and SST had different extents, resolutions, and origins, which were redefined using resample() and crop() for proper alignment.
Two different CRS between the three datasets:

depth: EPSG 4326
sst: EPSG 9122
eez_data: EPSG 9122

Since there were two datasets with the same CRS, the choice to change depth to match the others was decided.


Show code
# Crop data to match SST raster
crop_depth <- crop(depth, sst_mean_c)

# Transfer sst data using bilear method to match
resampled_depth <- resample(crop_depth, sst_mean_c, method = "bilinear")

# test if the resampled depth CRS matches the sst_mean_c CRS
  if (crs(resampled_depth) == crs(sst_mean_c)) {
    print("CRS match!")
  } else {
    warning("CRS don't match!")
    crs(resampled_depth) <- crs(sst_mean_c)
  }

title: Where in the Waters?
text:
Suitable location workflow
The following five steps are to build a function that will be used later to find suitable locations for marine species based on their sst and depth requirements.

Step 1. Reclassifying based on conditions
Both sst and depth were reclassified into 0’s and 1’s coinciding suitability of locations by creating a reclassification matrix.
Rows in the matrix are as following:

outside the lower range receive 0
suitable condition within range receives 1
outside the higher range recieve 0



Show code
# Variables for min and max SST
min_sst <- 11
max_sst <- 30

# SST reclassification matrix
  rcl_sst <- matrix(
    c(
      -Inf, min_sst, 0,
      min_sst, max_sst, 1,
      max_sst, Inf, 0
    ),
    ncol = 3,
    byrow = TRUE
  )

# Variables for min and max depth
min_depth <- 0
max_depth <- -70

# Depth reclassification matrix
rcl_depth <- matrix(
    c(
      -Inf, max_depth, 0,
      max_depth, min_depth, 1,
      min_depth, Inf, 0
    ),
    ncol = 3,
    byrow = TRUE
  )

# Reclassify sst and depth to suitable zones
zone_sst <- classify(sst_mean_c, rcl = rcl_sst)

zone_depth <- classify(resampled_depth, rcl = rcl_depth)

# Combine to adhere to satisfy both sst and depth for suitable zones
depth_sst_zones <- c(zone_sst, zone_depth)




Step 2. Combine with map algebra
After reclassification, a function for map alegbra using lapp() to layers as arguments.


Show code
zone_fun <- function(sst, depth){
  sst * depth
}
# Find suitable zones for oysters adhering to both conditions
suitable_zones <- lapp(depth_sst_zones,
 fun = zone_fun)




Step 3. Rasterize EEZ regions
EEZ data was rasterized by Region ID.


Show code
# Convert to raster
eez_raster <- rasterize(eez_data, suitable_zones, field = "rgn_id")


The EEZ raster values 1 through 5 are assigned as the following:

Oregon
Northern California
Central California
Southern California
Washington



Show code
plot(eez_raster, axes = FALSE) 





Exclusive Economic Zones on the West Coast






Step 4. Calculate the suitable areas within each EEZ region
Before moving onto any other spatial operations, cellSize() was used to compute the true area (km^2) of each cell to determine the suitable locations within EEZ.


Show code
# Calculate cell size
cell_size <- cellSize(suitable_zones, unit = "km", mask = TRUE)


Then set values to 0 that are outside the boundary and use only cells with value 1 to determing the suitable locations using mask().


Show code
# Use only the cells with value 1 as suitable in the total area
suitable_zmask <- mask(cell_size,suitable_zones, maskvalues = 0)


Use the zonal() operation to apply the sum of area using the EEZ raster and the masked suitable zones.


Show code
# Select raster cells by suitable zpmes inside EEZ
desired_zone <- zonal(suitable_zmask,eez_raster, fun = 'sum', na.rm = TRUE)


A table was created to show the total suitable area found inside EEZ for oysters.


Show code
desired_zone |> 
  kable(col.names = c("EEZ region", "Suitable area (km^2)")) |> 
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = "striped")

Step 5. Join results to EEZ regions and map suitable location
Before mapping, the suitable areas are inputted into a tibble to the left_join() with EEZ.


Show code
# Create a tibble
z_tibble <- as_tibble(desired_zone)

# Merge for desired zones to EEZ data
map_1 <- left_join(eez_data, z_tibble, by = "rgn_id")


A simple color palette was created for an aesthetically pleasing map of the West Coast.


Show code
# Creating a color palette to differentiate the regions
color_palette <- c("#d0f0f0", "#5fb3c7", "#1f78a8", "#08306b")


The first map for the oyster was confirmed to be accurate to the suitable locations determined by EEZ, though it is not shown here but instead shown further ahead.

      title = "Suitable Area (km²)",

  tm_options(component.autoscale = FALSE) +
  tm_title("Suitable Oyster Aquaculture\nin the West Coast by EEZ", size = 1)

title: Where in the Waters?
text:
Future direction

Demands: High demands on resources can intensify animal farming and inputs such as energy or ecosystem services like nutrient cycling (Hall et al. 2011).
Development: To further understand future development of marine aquaculture across the world, research and policy development is needed on the integration of growth potential with economic and social aspects that coincide with aquaculture (Gentry et al. 2017).
Consideration: Several communities are dependent on traditional fisheries and would benefit from consideration by integrating social, political, cultural, ecological dimensions into aquaculture planning where policymakers can practice expansion rather than replacement and support an equitable and sustainable seafood future ().

title: Where Climate meets Conflict
text:
Climate change affects those living and non-living across the globe without discrimination, impacting those who contribute the least. With the increase in natural disasters, scientists have been attempting to find a connection between climate change and violent conflict that arise from impacted resources and the inability to access basic essentials (Bowles et al., 2015). A study by Adams et al. (2018) states the biases that occur within these studies are overexaggerating the link between the two.
For a few years, scientists have been studying whether socioeconomic pressure from natural events due to climate change can create conflict and push communities to enact violence out of a neccesity to survive, but there is a bias from before data collection.



From: Sampling bias in climate–conflict research (Adams et al. 2018)


The figure above shows the continents that are mentioned the most when researching for communities that may have conflict due to climate change. As it shows, the continent of Africa is mentioned the most with South America being second.
A study based on Syria leading into its civil war crisis written by Bowles et al. (2015) when focusing on a drought that impacted the people with severe food insecurity. Syria, a country known for its political instability, was plagued by a drought from 2007 to 2010 that caused crop failures, decreased agricultural production across regions, as well as the cessation of government subsidies. This left about 1.5 million people, including refugees from Iraq, battling food insecurity. Discontent spread like fire, creating a ground for uprising, as the government remained incapable of providing relief to the people impacted by poverty. The timing of this coincides with the Syrian civil war occurring in 2011. The limitation for this paper was the fact that only Syria was studied even though the same drought impacted both Jordan and Lebanon. This is important for a true analysis on these connections which was mentioned in the article by Adams et al. (2018). There was little analysis on the two countries experiencing the same drought and the main question then transitions to studying whether the research claiming the connection between climate change and conflict was based on a sampling bias strategy. This question was conducted by scanning databases, searching articles based on geographic regions, economic levels, as well as agricultural contribution to GDP. A statistical analysis was also done to conclude that there was a sampling bias (Adams et al., 2018).
Adams et al. (2018) found that countries experiencing more than 1,000 battle-related deaths were mentioned about three times more in topics surrounding climate–conflict research compared to countries with fewer battle-related deaths. This can exaggerate the connection between the climate change and violent conflict which significantly impacts both scientific communities due to incomplete information as well as the harm vulnerable communities that are in need for public awareness and assistance. These studies such as the ones focusing on data with keywords using “conflict” to find published articles, can overemphasize the connection.
Beyond the incomplete representation, this can lead to stigmatization, such as people viewing some places as being more naturally violent than others. This stigmatization can hurt the appeal for investors or local people and international donors which can harm sustainable development. Therefore, leaving out areas without conflict can create a gap in knowledge on how people adapt to climate concerns and the impacts of it peacefully, which can be valuable for those in policymaking (Adams et al., 2018). These biases stemmed from scientists focusing on a few accessible regions, that were known for political instability, thus overstating the link between climate change and violent conflict.

Documentary on Environmental Veganism
Below is my research-based documentary:




For my Critical Thinking course (ES 40), we were tasked to do a research project of our choice and interest throughout the entire quarter. My question was based on the small percentage of students in my environmental classes identifying as vegan or vegetarian despite studies showing the amount of water and land usage that is put into upholding the meat and dairy industry. Thus, did veganism matter in the overall context of helping the Earth, if those who studied it did not partake in it?

Student interviews

title: Master of Environmental Data Science
section: A personal data collection and an interactive plot
text:
A personal data collection and an interactive plot
For a final project, we had to build an interactive plot using data we collected over the quarter. I chose to collect the dates and time I practiced yoga and the pain levels I experienced throughtout the week in terms of if I practived or not. This was a simple data collection, but was still great to use to become familiar with the R language.
Code below:

library(tidyverse)
library()
library(janitor)
library(htmlwidgets)


mydata <- read.csv("Data.csv") |>
  clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    tooltip_text = paste0(
      "Yoga Session: ", did_you_do_yoga, "<br>",
      "Pain Level After: ", pain_level_after)
  )

p <- ggplot(mydata, aes(
  x = did_you_do_yoga,
  y = pain_level_after,
  color = pain_level_after,
  text = tooltip_text
)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, size = 2.5, alpha = 0.6) +
  stat_summary(geom = "point", fun = mean, color = "#4a4a4a", size = 3) +
  scale_color_gradient(low = "#f9f871", high = "#7c3f98") +  # yellow to purple gradient
  labs(
    x = "Did You Do Yoga?",
    y = "Pain Level After Yoga",
    color = "Pain Level"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#ffe6eb", color = NA),        # baby pink background
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#ffffff", color = "#ffb6c1"), # white panel with pink border
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#ffccd5"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

plotly::ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text") |>
  plotly::layout(hoverlabel = list(font = list(size = 14)))

title: Monique Allyson Hernandez
text:
My Adventures around the world
The coolest thing to me when I was a kid was the idea of seeing the entire world, which is something I wanted to have my own child experience along with me. My family have origins from multiple parts of the world, including Mexico, South Korea, Portugal, and Spain.
My bucket list of places to visit has grown larger and larger as time goes on, but there are two places that are dear to me that take precedence. One is the birth place of my mom which is Jalisco, Mexico and the other is Seoul, South Korea where my paternal grandmother originates, though she was also born in Yucatan, Mexico.












France Trip 2022.

My favorite traveling memory is taking my 1 year old son to Europe and having him tag along everywhere we went like a 15 pound backpack! We stayed in Lyon, France and visited Paris as well as Geneva, Switzerland. His first playground he played on was a french playground and they really set the standard for playgrounds after that. Even more recently, we visited Tulum, Mexico where we spent all day at the pool or at the beach. And of course, no matter the location, my favorite thing to do is eat the local vegan food.

title: Monique Allyson Hernandez
text:
My Vegan Lifestyle



Homemade and Restaurant


I wasn’t born into a vegan life; I adopted one. I have always had a great interest in reducing my meat intake, cutting out dairy for health reasons, and just not harming animals in general, but never took the plunge until 2022.
People may think it’s just changing the diet, but it’s other things too like not buying fur, wool, or leather. My vegan lifestyle blends very well with my academic interests and I have had the chance to explore environmental veganism due to my major. There are many challenges that come with being vegan as the food may not be so easily accessible such as animal-based food, but with time and experience those challenges have become minimal. There are so many great dishes that have found their way into rotation. Currently, there’s a tuscan gnoochi dish that is comforting, filling, and delicious, but the best part is that it’s incredibly fast!
